extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants, patent prosecutors, and IP counsel preparing prosecution strategy before the USPTO
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on how the USPTO patent examiner production/count system works and how applicants can align prosecution strategy with examiner incentives to improve chances and speed of allowance. Focuses on expected production calculations, counts/production units, time allocations, and practical applicant tactics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner Annual Performance Rating (components)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent examiners' annual performance rating is based on a weighted average of four elements: Productivity (Production) — 35%; Quality — 35%; Docket management — 20%; Stakeholder interaction — 10%.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Production (number of production units) together with docket management (completion within an expected time frame) capture 55% of the weighted average; the article focuses on production and docket management. Quality and stakeholder interaction are also evaluated (separately referenced to USPTO quality assurance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Productivity (Production) metric
rubrics_metrics.description: Productivity is measured by the number of production units (PUs) an examiner produces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Production is evaluated based on counts/PUs (not actual hours spent). Examiners are incentivized to meet and exceed expected production, including via production award programs for exceeding 100%.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality (work and interactions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quality of examination work and interactions with internal and external contacts constitutes 35% of an examiner's rating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quality is a separate weighted component from production; applicants should be aware quality is evaluated but the count system emphasizes production counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Docket management
rubrics_metrics.description: Docket management accounts for 20% of the rating and means completion of production units within expected time frames.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Docket management measures timeliness relative to assigned expected-production schedules and is bundled with production as a major component of the examiner's appraisal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stakeholder interaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Stakeholder interaction comprises 10% of the annual rating and covers interactions with internal and external contacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This factor captures communication quality and engagement, which can affect evaluations but has less weight than production and quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formula for expected production (overview)
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO uses a formula to calculate expected production for a patent examiner, incorporating factors such as seniority factor, number of examining hours, and technical complexity (hours per production unit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding what drives expected production (and its components) allows applicants to predict examiner behavior and timing; baseline hours per PU vary by technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seniority factor (grade level)
rubrics_metrics.description: An examiner's GS grade level (GS-5 through GS-14, supervisory at GS-15) assigns a seniority factor that affects salary and the number of production units required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: GS-5 to GS-12 lack signatory authority; GS-13/14 may attain partial/full signatory authority; promotions to higher GS levels reduce the hours allocated per PU (e.g., promotion from GS-7 to GS-14 roughly halves hours per application).

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of examining hours
rubrics_metrics.description: Full-time examiners work 40 hours/week, but examining hours exclude training, staff meetings, and certain programs; typical examining hours are provided in USPTO tables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not all 40 hours count toward examination time; programs like After Final Consideration Pilot 2.0 provide additional examiner time; tables give typical examining hours used in expected production calculations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical complexity (hours per production unit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical complexity is expressed as baseline hours per production unit; more complex technologies are assigned more hours per PU.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Baseline expectancies range from about 13.8 to 31.6 hours per PU by CPC; examples: fishing lure ~16.6 hrs/PU, immunotherapy ~25.9 hrs/PU, satellite communication ~27.7 hrs/PU. USPTO continues to refine times considering claim count and IDS volume.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a Production Unit and Counts
rubrics_metrics.description: One production unit equals two counts; counts are awarded for certain prosecution actions, with a greater number of counts assigned to the first office action on the merits than to later actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A prosecution cycle typically includes two office actions and a disposal, but many applications have >2 office actions (RCEs), increasing counts. Tables translate counts into hours for different GS levels and technologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production measured in counts, not time
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiner production is evaluated based on PUs or counts (number of office actions issued), not the actual hours spent to issue those actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because compensation/awards depend on counts, examiners are encouraged to reduce time per office action; spending less than allocated time on an office action is contemplated and rewarded by production-award programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production award program (incentives to exceed 100%)
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO has a production award program that awards examiners for exceeding 100% production (example target includes 135% where achievable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Increasing production from 100% to 135% can require reducing time per count by roughly 25%; the award structure creates incentives for examiners to speed examination and produce more counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time allocation within prosecution cycles
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners have more time allocated to the beginning of each prosecution cycle (up to and including the first office action), and less time for later actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants can leverage this front-loaded time by prioritizing clarity and completeness early (e.g., in the initial filing, preliminary amendments, and first response).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of multiple office actions and RCEs on counts
rubrics_metrics.description: Where three or more office actions are issued, typically due to a request for continued examination (RCE), the examiner must take actions beyond the original prosecution cycle and additional counts/hours are assigned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High office_actions_per_grant ratios in some tech areas increase examiner counts and affect how examiners allocate time and produce PUs; applicants can avoid unnecessary RCEs to limit additional cycles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office Actions per Grant Ratio and other examiner-activity metrics (OGR, ODR, GER)
rubrics_metrics.description: Metrics such as Office Actions per Grant Ratio (OGR), Office Actions per Disposal Ratio (ODR), and Grant to Examiner Ratio (GER) are used to measure examiner activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These metrics contextualize how frequently examiners issue office actions relative to grants and disposals; awareness of these numbers helps applicants understand typical prosecution length in particular technology areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO updates to examination time and routing
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO is engaged in ongoing updates to examination time, application routing, and examiner performance appraisals, and considers application-specific factors (claim number, IDS volume) when refining times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants should be aware that baseline hours per PU and routing practices may change over time and that claim drafting and IDS management can influence the examiner's assigned time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategy: allocate greater effort to initial prosecution cycle
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants should allocate a greater amount of time and preparation to the initial prosecution cycle and actions at the beginning of each cycle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because examiners have more allocated time at the front of a cycle, preliminary amendments, early interviews, and thorough initial responses can leverage that time to resolve issues before later, lower-time phases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategy: minimize examiner time per action (make examination efficient)
rubrics_metrics.description: Design prosecution materials and responses to minimize the time an examiner needs to fully examine and allow an application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tactics include clear claim drafting aligned with commercial embodiments and U.S. law, concise yet complete responses, targeted prior-art explanations, and efficient use of interviews so the examiner can review and decide more quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategy: consider preliminary amendments before examination
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider submitting preliminary amendments to claims prior to examination to define invention scope in view of preferred commercial embodiments and U.S. law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is particularly useful when pendency before a first office action is long or when the application was drafted initially for another jurisdiction; it may reduce examiner time needed to understand and examine the claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategy: engage meaningfully and early with the examiner
rubrics_metrics.description: Engage with the examiner early in the initial prosecution cycle and provide a thoughtful and complete response to the first office action on the merits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early engagement (including interviews and clear responses) can prevent misunderstandings, save examiner time, and reduce the number of subsequent office actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategy: use interviews early and prepare a concise agenda
rubrics_metrics.description: Make use of interviews, particularly early during prosecution, and prepare a complete yet concise agenda prior to the interview.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A focused agenda helps the examiner rapidly prepare and makes efficient use of allocated interview time, increasing the chance of resolving issues quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategy: use USPTO programs that provide additional examiner time (e.g., After Final Consideration Pilot 2.0)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where appropriate, use USPTO programs that give examiners additional time (such as After Final Consideration Pilot 2.0) to obtain further consideration without filing an RCE.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These programs can provide opportunities to resolve issues while leveraging allocated additional examiner time, potentially avoiding full continuation practice that increases counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observation: viewing system through incentives/rational-maximizer lens
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand the count system from the perspective of a rational maximizer (an employee seeking to maximize compensation): examiners will respond to incentives embedded in the system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants can use this perspective to predict examiner behavior (e.g., preference for fewer hours per count, front-loaded effort) and tailor prosecution strategy accordingly.
